title: Ulu Cami, Koza Han and the Hanlar district
tagline: Twenty domes, a silk caravanserai with tea in the courtyard, and a covered bazaar that still sells things people need — the Ottoman capital in one walk.
when: weekday morning — outside prayer times for the mosque
why: Bursa was the first Ottoman capital, and the Hanlar district — inscribed by UNESCO in 2014 together with Cumalıkızık — is where that city still functions. Ulu Cami, built in the 1390s, is the biggest thing here: twenty domes over a single hall, a fountain indoors under an open skylight, and the walls covered in enormous calligraphy, so it feels like walking into a book. Across the street, Koza Han (1491) is the caravanserai where the silk cocoon trade was done for five centuries, and the courtyard is now the city's best tea garden. Around both, the Kapalıçarşı and its side hans still sell towels, knives, fabric and silk to Bursalılar, not to tour groups.
take: This is the first walk we do with every newcomer. Start in Ulu Cami between prayer times (mornings are calmest), sit under the domes for longer than feels reasonable, then cross to Koza Han for a çay in the courtyard — the ritual is the point. Drift through the covered bazaar and into the hans behind it without a plan; Kayhan Çarşısı, a few minutes away, is where İskender kebap was invented. One honesty note: Osmangazi municipality announced a Koza Han restoration in June 2026, then postponed it and the café tables came back — ⚠ VERIFY the courtyard cafés are open before you promise anyone a tea there.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: Ulu Cami — the indoor şadırvan under the skylight, and the calligraphy on every pier.
Koza Han courtyard — tea under the plane trees, silk scarves in the shops upstairs.
The Kapalıçarşı and the smaller hans behind it (Emir Han, Fidan Han) — still a working market.
A stop at Kafkas in Heykel, candied Uludağ chestnuts since 1930 — the city's sweet.
Cover shoulders and knees in the mosque; women bring a scarf. Step out for prayer times.

title: The Green Tomb, the Green Mosque and the Irgandı bridge
tagline: Turquoise tiles on a hill above the Gökdere, then a bridge with shops built on it — the prettiest corner of old Bursa.
when: late afternoon — the tiles catch the low light
why: Up the hill east of the Gökdere stream stands the Yeşil complex: the Green Mosque (1414–1419), built for Mehmed I with an interior of blue-green tilework that gives the whole quarter its name, and the Green Tomb opposite, a turquoise-tiled octagon that is Bursa's most photographed building. The old medrese beside them houses the Turkish and Islamic Arts museum. Walk back down toward Setbaşı and you cross the Gökdere on the Irgandı bridge — built in 1442 with shops on top of it, one of a handful of inhabited bridges left in the world, rebuilt to its old form in 2004 and now full of small craft workshops.
take: Come in the last two hours of daylight: the tiles on the tomb go from blue to green as the sun drops, and the mosque is quiet between afternoon and evening prayers. Give the tomb ten minutes inside, then let the streets pull you downhill — Setbaşı has the cafés and the view back up to Yeşil. Cross the Irgandı bridge slowly and talk to whoever is working in the shops; it's tiny and that's the charm. Our favorite Bursa ending to a first day.

sections.title: Good to know
items: The mosque is a working one — visit outside prayer times, dress modestly, shoes off.
Tomb and mosque are free; the museum in the medrese is a modest ticket.
Setbaşı bridge and the cafés along the Gökdere are the natural place to stop afterwards.

title: İskender kebap where it was invented
tagline: Bursa's dish, eaten in Bursa: sliced döner on pide, tomato sauce, yogurt, and butter poured on at the table.
when: lunchtime — it's a midday dish here
why: The vertical döner spit was invented in this city. In 1867 İskender Efendi, working in Kayhan Çarşısı, stood the meat upright over charcoal, sliced it thin and served it on torn pide with tomato sauce and yogurt — and the dish that every Turkish restaurant abroad now serves is named after him. His descendants, the İskenderoğlu family, still run the historic shops in and around Heykel; there are two lines of the family, each with 1867 on the sign, and the city argues gently about which is truer. Either way you're eating the original in the only place that can claim it.
take: Do this in your first week, at lunch, in one of the family's old shops rather than a franchise in a mall — the room matters. Order the kebap and a glass of şıra (fermented grape juice, the traditional pairing), and wait for the waiter to pour the browned butter over the plate; that moment is the whole ceremony. Then walk it off through the bazaar. If you've only had İskender elsewhere, this resets the dish. The rest of Bursa's table is below — work through it over your first month.

sections.title: The rest of the Bursa table
items: Kestane şekeri — candied chestnuts from Uludağ's slopes; Kafkas in Heykel has made them since 1930.
Pideli köfte and İnegöl köfte — the two other grills the city is proud of.
Cantık — Bursa's small, closed pide, a lunch in your hand.
Kemalpaşa tatlısı — a syrupy cheese sweet from the town of the same name, sold everywhere in the center.
Roasted chestnuts on the street from October — the smell of a Bursa autumn.

title: A thermal hamam in Çekirge
tagline: Hot mineral water that sultans came for — in a 1385 bath under a dome, a short bus ride from the center.
why: Bursa sits on hot springs, and Çekirge and Kükürtlü on the western slope are where the water comes up — the reason the Ottomans built here and the reason the neighborhood is full of thermal hotels. Two historic baths anchor it: Eski Kaplıca, built for Murad I in 1385 on a Byzantine bath and today run as part of the Kervansaray thermal hotel, and Yeni Kaplıca in Kükürtlü, built by Rüstem Paşa in 1552 after the spring eased Süleyman's gout. Both are hamams the old way — hot marble, a domed pool of genuinely hot mineral water, separate sections for men and women — and both are things the city actually uses, not heritage props.
take: Save this for the first cold snap; a Bursa winter afternoon in a hot-spring pool under a five-hundred-year-old dome is the argument for living here. Go with a small group — hamams are sociable, and this is one of our easiest 'meet people' outings — and bring flip-flops and your own towel to be safe. The practical bit we can't confirm from a distance: ⚠ VERIFY current day-visitor hours and the men's/women's arrangement at both baths before you go (Eski Kaplıca's thermal section lists 07:00–22:00 daily, but that page is written for hotel guests). Ask at the door; they're used to newcomers.

title: Sunset at the Tophane clock tower
tagline: Tea on the terrace where the empire's founders are buried, the whole plain below and Uludağ turning pink behind you.
why: Tophane is the citadel hill Bursa was founded on, and its park is the city's balcony: the Bursa plain spread out to the north, the center directly below, and the mass of Uludağ rising behind. On it stand the tombs of Osman Gazi and Orhan Gazi — the founder of the Ottoman dynasty and the son who took Bursa in 1326 — and the 1905 clock tower, 33 metres of Ottoman civic pride that has become the city's symbol. The square around them was renovated recently and the tea gardens along the edge face the view.
take: This is the free, no-plan evening we send everyone to first. Come up an hour before sunset, look into the two tombs (free, quick, quietly moving), then take a table at the edge with a çay and stay until the lights come on across the plain. It pairs perfectly with a wander down through Muradiye's old streets afterwards, or up from the bazaar beforehand. Half of what we know about Bursa we learned from strangers at these tables.

title: Take the teleferik up Uludağ
tagline: From a city street to alpine forest in half an hour — nearly nine kilometres of gondola line, and a picnic at the top.
when: a clear day — check it's running before you leave
why: Bursa is the only big Turkish city with a mountain on its doorstep, and the teleferik is how the city gets up it: gondolas from the Teferrüç station on the eastern edge of town, up through Kadıyayla to the Sarıalan meadows in the national park, and on to the hotel zone near the ski lifts. The line was completely rebuilt as a modern gondola in 2014 and, at nearly nine kilometres, is one of the longest cable-car routes anywhere. Sarıalan at the top is what it sounds like — a high forest clearing with picnic tables, tea gardens and walking paths, and cool air when the city below is baking.
take: Pick a clear day (the ride is the view) and get off at Sarıalan rather than riding to the end: the meadow is the experience, and a slow tea in the pines beats the hotel zone. Bring layers — it is a different climate up there in any month. The line runs daily, roughly ten to seven as of late summer 2026, but wind, fog and maintenance close it without much notice, so ⚠ VERIFY it's operating on the day (phone or the operator's site) before you gather a group. It's a private concession, so it sells its own tickets — don't count on a BursaKart at the gate. A great first Smileys outing: small group, one gondola, lots of talking.

sections.title: Stations, bottom to top
items: Teferrüç — the base station on the eastern edge of the city; reachable by city bus.
Kadıyayla — a mid-station in the forest.
Sarıalan — the meadow, the picnic tables, the walking trails. Get off here.
Oteller (hotel zone) — the ski lifts and hotels; the top of the line.

title: Uludağ in two seasons: walks and snow
tagline: A 2,500-metre national park above the city — forest trails and yayla picnics in summer, Turkey's oldest ski resort in winter.
when: May–October for walking; roughly mid-December to March for snow
why: Uludağ — the Mysian Olympus of the ancients — is a national park that starts at the edge of the city and climbs to over 2,500 metres. In the warm months it is Bursa's back garden: the Sarıalan and Kirazlıyayla meadows for picnics and camping, forest paths between them, and viewpoints like Bakacak where the whole plain and, on a clear day, the Marmara open out below. From December it becomes the country's oldest ski resort, with the hotel zones, lifts and a Turkish winter-weekend culture all of its own. Living in Bursa means having both an hour away.
take: Summer first: take the teleferik or a shared car to Sarıalan, walk the marked paths between the yaylas, and picnic like the locals do — this is the easiest group day out we know, and it needs no gear beyond real shoes and water. Leave the summit ridges to a proper mountain day with someone who knows it; the weather turns fast. In winter, be honest about what you want: the slopes are busy and pricey on weekends, and a weekday snow walk around Sarıalan with a hot salep is the version most of us prefer. Ski season dates move with the snow — ⚠ VERIFY opening before planning a trip around it.

title: Village breakfast in Cumalıkızık
tagline: A 700-year-old Ottoman village on the mountain's foot — cobbled lanes, timber houses, and the longest breakfast of your week.
when: a weekday morning — weekends are a crush
why: Cumalıkızık was one of the first villages the early Ottomans settled on the slopes of Uludağ, and seven centuries later it still has its shape: steep cobbled lanes, timber-and-plaster houses in ochre and blue with overhanging upper floors, and a village square under trees. It is on the UNESCO list with Bursa's old center for exactly that reason. The way the village lives now is breakfast — courtyards and house-gardens serving the whole spread, homemade jams, village bread, gözleme off the griddle, honey from the mountain — and it's a twenty-minute drive from the city.
take: Go on a weekday and go early: on a weekend afternoon the lanes are shoulder to shoulder and the food gets rushed. Pick a courtyard place rather than one on the main lane, order the full village spread for the table (it's a shared meal — the whole point), and then walk the upper lanes, which most people never reach. This is our standard 'welcome to Bursa' morning for a new group: unhurried, cheap for what it is, and everyone leaves full and friends.

title: Mudanya: the seafront, and the boat from Istanbul
tagline: Bursa's port town on the Marmara — a long promenade, fish by the water, and the sea bus that makes Istanbul a day trip.
when: late afternoon — walk, then fish at sunset
why: Half an hour north of the city, Mudanya is where Bursa meets the sea: an old Greek and Ottoman port with a long waterfront promenade, stone houses on the slope, and fish restaurants along the front. It's also the reason many of us live here — the sea buses tie Bursa to Istanbul without a bus or a bridge. BUDO, run by Bursa's own transit company, sails from Mudanya to Kabataş (its Istanbul end moved there from Eminönü on 1 January 2026; the crossing is under two hours), and İDO's Yenikapı–Bursa fast ferry lands at the Güzelyalı pier just west of town. The armistice that ended the Turkish War of Independence was signed here in 1922, and the house is a small museum on the front.
take: Do Mudanya as an evening: ride out on a summer afternoon, walk the whole promenade, look into the Mütareke Evi, and sit down to fish and a glass of something as the sun goes down over the gulf. In winter the town is quiet and local, which is its own charm. For Istanbul, the sea bus is the civilised way — book ahead on busy weekends, and remember it's a separate reserved-seat ticket, not a tap of your transit card. Our members who commute say the ride is the best part of the week.

sections.title: Getting to and from the boat
items: BUDO — Mudanya pier to Kabataş, Istanbul; tickets online, in the BUDO app or at the pier.
İDO — Yenikapı, Istanbul to Bursa (Güzelyalı pier, west of Mudanya).
City buses run between Mudanya, Güzelyalı and central Bursa; allow a full hour door to door.

title: Tirilye, the stone village
tagline: A Greek-built olive town on the coast west of Mudanya — churches turned mosques, a stone school, and the best olives you'll buy from a doorway.
why: Along the coast from Mudanya, Tirilye is a small town built up two sides of a valley by its Greek population and made rich by olives — it was officially renamed Zeytinbağı, 'olive orchard', from 1963 until it got its old name back in 2012. What remains is a tight village of stone houses, three Byzantine churches in various afterlives (one the Fatih mosque, one the arched Kemerli Kilise), a grand stone school building, and lanes that drop to a small harbor. Everyone here sells olives and oil, and everyone's is the best.
take: Come in the shoulder seasons when the light is soft and the lanes are empty, and let the town be small: an hour of wandering, a coffee by the harbor, a plate of fish or a village lunch, and olives to take home. It chains naturally with Mudanya on the way back for the seafront and dinner. A good low-effort Smileys half-day — you can do it with a shared car and no plan at all.

title: Gölyazı and the lake
tagline: An island village on Uluabat lake — a 750-year-old plane tree, storks on the roofs, and a boat out among the lilies.
when: spring, when the storks are back — or any calm afternoon
why: West of the city on Uluabat lake, Gölyazı is an old Greek fishing village on what was an island, now joined to the shore — stone houses, a ruined church of St Panteleimon, nets drying on the quay, and storks nesting on every chimney from spring. At the entrance stands the Ağlayan Çınar, the 'weeping plane tree', around 750 years old, with a tea garden underneath and the lake beyond. Boats take you out onto the water among the reed beds and water lilies; the lake is a wetland of real importance for birds.
take: Sit under the plane tree first — tea, lake, nothing else — then walk the village lanes and out along the shore to the Zambaktepe viewpoint for the panorama. If it's calm, take a boat: the lake is the point, and half an hour out on it is the quietest place within reach of Bursa. Spring is the season, for the storks and the wildflowers; in winter the village is mostly closed up. A perfect slow Sunday for a small group.

title: İznik: the lake, the walls and the tiles
tagline: Ancient Nicaea — Roman walls you can still walk through, the church of the councils, and the workshops that make the tiles the world knows.
when: a weekend day — finish on the lakeshore at sunset
why: An hour and a half east, on the shore of its own lake, İznik is Nicaea: the city of the first Christian ecumenical council, of the Byzantine court in exile, of the early Ottomans — and of the famous blue-and-white tiles. The Roman-Byzantine walls still ring the town and you drive in through their gates. In the center, the Ayasofya where the seventh council met is now the Orhan mosque, open and free, its mosaics and frescoes still visible. A new museum building opened in 2023 for the archaeological finds, the excavated Ottoman tile kilns sit behind the Ayasofya as an open-air site, and working tile studios sell what they make. Then there is the lake itself, huge and calm, with tea gardens along the shore.
take: Make it a full day and don't rush the walls — walk the İstanbul and Lefke gates, then the center on foot. Buy tiles from a studio, not a stall, and talk to the maker; this is a craft that was nearly lost and revived. Eat by the lake, and stay for sunset on the shore, which is the moment İznik earns the drive. Best done with a shared car for a group of four or five — it's one of our favorite Smileys road days from Bursa.

title: Gemlik, olive country
tagline: The black table olive the whole country asks for by name — buy it in the town it's named after, at harvest if you can.
why: Say 'Gemlik zeytini' anywhere in Turkey and people know what you mean: the small, black, oily table olive that sits on every breakfast table in the country. It has carried a Turkish geographical indication since 2003 and in 2023 became the first Turkish olive registered by the European Union. Gemlik itself is a working town at the head of the gulf, half an hour from Bursa, ringed by groves that climb the hills — and from November the whole area is picking, brining and selling. The producers around İznik and Orhangazi are inside the same protected region.
take: Go during the harvest — the town smells of it, and buying a season's olives straight from a producer, tasting from the barrel first, is a small Bursa rite. Ask for the salamura (brine-cured) and the yağlı (oil-cured) and learn the difference; then ask for the oil. Pair it with Tirilye along the coast or with İznik inland for a full day. Newcomers who do this once stop buying olives in supermarkets.

title: A night out in Görükle
tagline: Bursa's student town beside the university — cheap plates, live music, and a crowd that is twenty-two and talking to strangers.
when: a term-time Thursday or Friday, from 8pm
why: Uludağ University's main campus sits out in Nilüfer, and Görükle, the town at its gate, is where tens of thousands of students live, eat and go out. It has its own rhythm, separate from the center's: cafés open until late, pubs with live music, cheap and good student food, and the loosest, most talkative crowd in the city. For a newcomer under thirty-five — or anyone who wants a Bursa night that isn't a mall — this is where the energy is.
take: Term time only; in summer it empties out. Start with a plate of something cheap and filling, find whichever bar has a band, and stay open to the table next to you — in Görükle people talk, which is exactly why we like it for Smileys evenings. It's a fair way out, so go with a group and sort the ride home before you start. Don't expect polish; expect a good time.

title: Green Bursa: Kültürpark, the Nilüfer stream and the Botanik Park
tagline: Three big parks for a city that calls itself 'green Bursa' — a walk, a run, a picnic, and on match days the roar next door.
why: Yeşil Bursa, 'green Bursa', is an old nickname the city is still trying to live up to, and three parks do most of the work. Kültürpark, at Altıparmak on the edge of Çekirge, is the classic city park — forty hectares of old trees, ponds, tea gardens, the open-air theatre where summer concerts happen, and the archaeology museum. Hüdavendigar Kent Parkı, west of Çekirge along the Nilüfer stream, is the biggest green space in the city: long paths, sports fields, canoeing on the stream. And the Botanik Park in Soğanlı, laid out in 1998, is the quiet one — themed gardens, a small zoo, bike paths. Rising over the Kent Parkı is the crocodile-shaped stadium where Bursaspor plays.
take: Start with Kültürpark on a weekday evening — it's where the center goes to walk, and the tea gardens are where you end up. Save Hüdavendigar for a run or a Sunday picnic with a group; it's big enough to feel like leaving town. And if you want to meet Bursa at full volume, go to a Bursaspor match: the club won the 2. Lig in 2025–26 and is back in the 1. Lig for 2026–27, the green-and-white crowd is the city's most loyal, and the stadium is next to the park. A match, then a walk along the stream — that's a proper Bursa Saturday.
